findings.proposed_fix: Replace the field with: 'On Mount Athos monks had long practiced hesychia, or stillness. They sat alone, held the breath steady, and repeated the Jesus Prayer until it went on by itself. Some of them said they saw an uncreated light. The Calabrian scholar Barlaam mocked the practice. Gregory Palamas, an Athonite monk who later became archbishop of Thessalonica, answered him in the Triads. God cannot be known in his essence, he argued, and yet he is truly given in his energies. So what the praying monk meets is God himself, not some created stand-in. The argument ran for two decades. Councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 settled it in Palamas's favor, and the hesychast view became the standard of Orthodox theology. Beside it stands a very different voice. Nicholas Cabasilas, a layman of Thessalonica, wrote The Life in Christ. He showed that the same life in God came through the sacraments to people who would never enter a monastery.' (Reading Ease 60.2, FK 8.1; no fact added or dropped.)

All 43 new links name their text in named_in, and I checked each against the census fields. All 21 earlier links touching era-6 movements are named in one end's text: Joachim is in the joachimite-current legacy, the Templars in the papacy summary, the Carthusians in the English mystics summary. The other relationships named in era-6 text have a link, a qualification, a removal or a stated no-entry or not-a-claim reason in the dispositions. One exception is R1-05: there the removals were the wrong disposition for plain facts.
notes: Method. A script compared every one of the 150 sourced quotes in the 43 new links against its file at the cited lines, joining wrapped lines with single spaces. All 150 match. Separately, I read each quote in context, a few lines either side, for all 43 links, and judged whether it shows the relationship and not just the events. The census edges and the drafting record agree field for field for all 43 links. No pre-existing edge was changed or removed. Scope holds: every new link has an era-6 end. Symmetric links are in alphabetical order. Each pair with two links (Hussites and Taborites; the order and the fraticelli; the papacy and the Franciscan order) carries two separately evidenced claims. No duplicate has the same type and direction as a published link. Questions put to me: (1) Lollardy to the English Reformation: Documented holds, as hussite--lutheran did (R1-08). (2) Tabor 1452 meets the outcome test, basis (c). Lützow 10147-10149, on the link and read, has the regent forcibly impose the Utraquist service, which is a practice changed by an authority. Lützow calls George regent at 10132-10133. (3) Florence meets the test, basis (c). Laetentur caeli is a council's settlement, not a letter, and Leonard (54517-54518) shows the union proclaimed at Constantinople in 1452. (4) The 1448 Jonah outcome is shown by its own source, but needs rewording (R1-17). (5) Leave the Capistrano and Breslau sentence standing and log it (R1-24). (6) The hesychasm fragments are real, and the field also fails readability (R1-06). (7) Group E's removals of plain facts are inconsistent with era-5 practice and with groups A and C, so restore them and log them (R1-05). Group E's corrections that follow its sources are right and stay: the patriarchs at Gazarta and Mosul, not a mountain village; family succession dated by the sixteenth century; and the Roman record on the Maronites' one-will teaching. (8) Hakkari: the fields are now correct, the teaser overstates, and the name is Mark's call (R1-23). Other checks that passed. Ethiopian and Armenian 'continued as' stay Documented on the era-5 precedent (R1-11), under which later texts can carry a continuity if the note says they are late. Both notes say so: Mendes 'a hundred years later', Zakaria 'wrote in the 1600s'.
